cse-2025-1-cs-4.approach: A (single-level) page table has one entry per **virtual** page. So split the 32-bit logical address into page number and offset; the number of entries is $2^{\text{page-number bits}}$. The physical address size only decides how wide each entry is.
cse-2025-1-cs-4.given:
| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| logical address | 32 bits |
| physical address | 20 bits |
| page size | $2048$ B $= 2^{11}$ B |
| addressing | byte addressable |

steps.title: Offset bits from the page size
steps.body: Byte addressable, page size $2048 = 2^{11}$ bytes, so the offset field needs $\log_2 2048 = 11$ bits.

steps.title: Page-number bits from the logical address
steps.body:
Page number $= 32 - 11 = 21$ bits, so the logical address space has
$$\frac{2^{32}}{2^{11}} = 2^{32-11} = 2^{21} \text{ pages.}$$

steps.title: One page-table entry per virtual page
steps.body:
The page table is indexed by the page number, so it must be able to hold an entry for every virtual page: maximum entries $= 2^{21}$.

The 20-bit physical address only fixes the frame-number width: $20 - 11 = 9$ bits per entry (plus control bits). It does **not** change the number of entries.

scene.caption: Entries depend on the logical side; entry width on the physical side

optionAnalysis.reason: $2^{32}/2^{11} = 2^{21}$ virtual pages, one entry each.
$2^{20}$ is the number of bytes of physical memory (20-bit physical address), not the number of pages.
$2^{22}$ would need a 1024-byte page ($32 - 10 = 22$); the page here is 2048 bytes.
$2^{24}$ corresponds to a 256-byte page ($32 - 8$); it does not follow from the given data.

cse-2025-1-cs-4.shortcut: Entries $= \dfrac{\text{virtual address space}}{\text{page size}} = 2^{32-11} = 2^{21}$; ignore the physical address size.
pitfalls: Using the physical address (20 bits) to count page-table entries — that gives the number of frames ($2^9$), which sets the entry width only.
Taking the offset as 2048 bits or 12 bits instead of $\log_2 2048 = 11$.
cse-2025-1-cs-4.verification: Check: $2^{21}$ pages $\times 2^{11}$ B/page $= 2^{32}$ B, exactly the logical address space.

cse-2025-1-cs-5.approach: When $T_1$ aborts, every transaction that **read a value written by $T_1$** (a dirty read) must also roll back — cascading rollback. So find the items $T_1$ wrote and who read them afterwards.

steps.title: What did T1 write?
steps.body: $T_1$ performs $R_1(X)$ and $W_1(Y)$. Its only write is to $Y$. Reading $X$ creates no dependency: $X$ was never changed, so $R_2(X)$ reads the committed/original value.

steps.title: T2 reads Y written by T1
steps.body: $R_2(Y)$ comes after $W_1(Y)$ with no other write to $Y$ in between, so $T_2$ reads the uncommitted value of $Y$ written by $T_1$ ($T_2$ reads-from $T_1$). When $T_1$ aborts, that value never existed, so **$T_2$ must roll back**.

steps.title: T3 also reads Y written by T1
steps.body: $R_3(Y)$ also follows $W_1(Y)$ with no intervening write (reads by $T_2$ do not change $Y$). So $T_3$ also read $T_1$'s dirty value: **$T_3$ must roll back** too.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Abort of $T_1$ $\Rightarrow$ cascading rollback of $T_2$ and $T_3$. (Neither has committed, so the schedule is still recoverable — it is just not cascadeless.)

answer.value: **Both $T_2$ and $T_3$** must be rolled back — option (C)

optionAnalysis.reason: Misses $T_3$: $R_3(Y)$ also reads the value written by $W_1(Y)$.
Misses $T_2$: $R_2(Y)$ reads $T_1$'s uncommitted $Y$ as well.
$T_2$ and $T_3$ both read-from $T_1$ via $Y$, so both cascade.
Wrong: looking only at $X$ (which $T_1$ just read) ignores the dirty reads of $Y$.

pitfalls: Thinking $R_2(X)$ creates a dependency — reading an item that $T_1$ only *read* is harmless.
Assuming $T_3$ reads from $T_2$ rather than $T_1$: $T_2$ never wrote $Y$, so the last writer of $Y$ before $R_3(Y)$ is still $T_1$.
cse-2025-1-cs-5.verification: Last writer before each read: $R_2(X)$ → initial value; $R_2(Y)$ → $T_1$; $R_3(Y)$ → $T_1$. Exactly the reads with last writer $T_1$ cascade: $T_2$, $T_3$.

cse-2025-1-cs-6.approach: Recall the one-line job of each layer: network = routing packets across networks, transport = end-to-end (host-to-host/process-to-process) delivery, data link = framing and error handling on one link.

steps.title: Network layer → packet routing
steps.body: The network layer (IP) chooses paths across the internetwork and forwards packets hop by hop: **(a)–(I)**.

steps.title: Transport layer → host to host communication
steps.body: The transport layer (TCP/UDP) provides end-to-end communication between the two hosts (their processes), with ports, reliability and flow control: **(b)–(III)**.

steps.title: Data link layer → framing and error handling
steps.body:
The data link layer packs bits into frames, and detects/handles errors on a single link (CRC, retransmission in link protocols): **(c)–(II)**.

So the matching is (a)-(I), (b)-(III), (c)-(II).

optionAnalysis.reason: Gives framing to the transport layer and host-to-host delivery to the data link layer — swapped.
Routing → network, end-to-end → transport, framing → data link.
Routing is not a data-link job and framing is not a network-layer job.
Host-to-host delivery is not the network layer's role in this matching, and the data link layer does not route packets.

pitfalls: Reading "host to host" as the network layer's job: in OSI terms the end-to-end (host-to-host) layer is transport; the network layer does the hop-by-hop routing.
cse-2025-1-cs-6.verification: Each functionality is used exactly once and each layer gets exactly its textbook job; only option (B) does this.

cse-2025-1-cs-7.approach: Ontoness of $f \circ g$ only says every $c \in C$ is hit through *some* element of $B$; $g$ may miss elements of $B$ or merge elements of $A$. One tiny counterexample that is neither one-to-one nor onto settles it.

steps.title: What the hypothesis really gives
steps.body: $f \circ g$ onto means: for every $c \in C$ there is $a \in A$ with $f(g(a)) = c$. This already forces $f$ onto (take $b = g(a)$). It says nothing about the elements of $B$ that are **not** of the form $g(a)$, and nothing about how many $a$ map to the same $b$.

steps.title: Build a counterexample
steps.body:
Take $A = \{1, 2\}$, $B = \{p, q\}$, $C = \{c\}$, with
$g(1) = g(2) = p$ and $f(p) = f(q) = c$.

- $f$ is onto ($c$ is hit).
- $f(g(1)) = f(g(2)) = c$, so $f \circ g$ is onto.

steps.title: g is neither one-to-one nor onto
steps.body:
- $g(1) = g(2) = p$ with $1 \ne 2$, so $g$ is **not injective**.
- $q \in B$ has no preimage under $g$, so $g$ is **not surjective**.

Hence none of "must be onto", "must be one-to-one", "must be bijective" is forced: $g$ is not required to be either.

answer.value: **$g$ is not required to be one-to-one or onto** — option (D)

optionAnalysis.reason: False: in the example $q \in B$ is never hit by $g$, yet $f$ and $f \circ g$ are onto. (Onto-ness of $f \circ g$ forces $f$ onto, not $g$.)
False: $g(1) = g(2)$ in the example. Injectivity of $g$ would follow from $f \circ g$ being **one-to-one**, which is not given.
False: bijective needs both, and the example has neither.
True: the counterexample satisfies the hypotheses with $g$ neither injective nor surjective.

cse-2025-1-cs-7.shortcut: Remember the true facts: $f \circ g$ onto $\Rightarrow$ $f$ onto; $f \circ g$ one-to-one $\Rightarrow$ $g$ one-to-one. Nothing is forced on $g$ by ontoness.
pitfalls: Swapping the roles of $f$ and $g$: the outer function inherits ontoness, the inner one inherits injectivity.
cse-2025-1-cs-7.verification: Every hypothesis is checked on the concrete sets ($|C| = 1$ makes every map into $C$ onto), and each of (A), (B), (C) fails on the same example.

cse-2025-1-cs-8.approach: The $u$–$v$ path in $T$ is also a path in $G$, so $d_1 \le d_2$ always. A three-vertex example shows the inequality can be strict and can be equality, killing (A), (C), (D).

steps.title: Why d1(u,v) ≤ d2(u,v) always
steps.body: $T$ is a subgraph of $G$ (same vertices, a subset of edges with the same weights). The unique $u$–$v$ path in $T$ has length $d_2(u,v)$ and is also a $u$–$v$ path in $G$. The shortest path in $G$ can only be shorter or equal, so $d_1(u,v) \le d_2(u,v)$.

steps.title: Example: the MST of a triangle
steps.body: Let $G$ be a triangle with $w(u,v) = 3$, $w(u,w) = 2$, $w(v,w) = 2$. The MST takes the two cheapest edges: $T = \{uw, vw\}$ with weight $2 + 2 = 4$.

steps.title: Strict inequality for u, v
steps.body: $d_1(u,v) = 3$ (direct edge), but in $T$ the only path is $u - w - v$: $d_2(u,v) = 2 + 2 = 4$. So $d_1 < d_2$: options (A) and (C) are false.

steps.title: Equality for u, w
steps.body: $d_1(u,w) = 2$ and $d_2(u,w) = 2$ (the tree edge $uw$). So equality is possible and option (D) ($\ne$ always) is false. Only $d_1 \le d_2$ holds for all $G, T, u, v$.

optionAnalysis.reason: False: in the triangle, $d_1(u,v) = 3 \ne 4 = d_2(u,v)$. An MST minimises total weight, not pairwise distances.
True: the tree path is a path in $G$, so the shortest $G$-path is no longer.
False: it would need the tree path to beat the shortest path in $G$, impossible since $T \subseteq G$ (and $3 < 4$ in the example).
False: for the endpoints of any MST edge on a shortest path, e.g. $u, w$ above, both distances are equal.

pitfalls: Confusing an MST with a shortest-path tree: the MST need not contain shortest paths between all pairs.
cse-2025-1-cs-8.verification: Kruskal on the triangle: pick $uw$ (2), $vw$ (2), reject $uv$ (3, cycle). Distances recomputed: $d_1(u,v) = \min(3, 4) = 3$, $d_2(u,v) = 4$.

cse-2025-1-cs-9.approach: Read off what each variable generates ($A \Rightarrow^* a^n$, $B \Rightarrow^* b^n$, $n \ge 1$), then substitute into the two $S$-rules. Each rule fixes one side to exactly two symbols.

steps.title: What A and B generate
steps.body:
$A \to a \mid aA$ generates $a, aa, aaa, \dots$, i.e. $L(A) = \{a^n \mid n \ge 1\}$.
$B \to b \mid bB$ generates $L(B) = \{b^n \mid n \ge 1\}$.

steps.title: Rule S → aaB
steps.body: $S \to aaB$ gives $aa \cdot b^n = a^2 b^n$, $n \ge 1$: exactly two $a$'s followed by one or more $b$'s. Example tree: $aabbb$.

steps.title: Rule S → Abb
steps.body: $S \to Abb$ gives $a^n \cdot bb = a^n b^2$, $n \ge 1$: one or more $a$'s followed by exactly two $b$'s. Example tree: $aaabb$.

steps.title: Union of the two rules
steps.body:
$$L(G) = \{a^2 b^n \mid n \ge 1\} \cup \{a^n b^2 \mid n \ge 1\}$$
Every string has exactly two $a$'s or exactly two $b$'s — option (A).

optionAnalysis.reason: Exactly the union of the languages of the two $S$-rules.
Contains $a^3 b^6$ ($n = 3$ in $a^n b^{2n}$), which has neither exactly two $a$'s nor exactly two $b$'s, so $G$ cannot derive it; and $a^2 b^3 \in L(G)$ is not of either form.
$a^3 b^3 \notin L(G)$, while $aab \in L(G)$ has unequal counts. The grammar never matches counts.
$a^4 b^4 \notin L(G)$, and $aab \in L(G)$ is not of the form $a^{2n} b^{2n}$.

pitfalls: Thinking a CFG with two recursive variables must "count" $a$'s against $b$'s: here $A$ and $B$ recurse independently, so there is no matching of counts.
cse-2025-1-cs-9.verification: Smallest strings of $G$: $aab, aabb$ (from both rules), $abb$, $aaabb$, $aabbb$ — all of the form in (A); and every string of (A) is derived by the matching rule.

cse-2025-1-cs-10.approach: Divide by $2^n$: with $U(n) = T(n)/2^n$ the recurrence becomes $U(n) = U(n-1) + n$, a plain sum. This gives the exact closed form, so the $\Theta$ bound is immediate.

steps.title: Back to T(n)
steps.body:
$$T(n) = 2^n\left(1 + \frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right) = 2^n \cdot \frac{n^2 + n + 2}{2}.$$
The dominant term is $\tfrac{1}{2} n^2 2^n$, so $T(n) = \Theta(n^2 2^n)$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Exact solution $2^n(n^2 + n + 2)/2 = \Theta(n^2 2^n)$.
Too small: that is only the size of the last added term $n2^n$; the $n$ levels each contribute $k2^n$, summing to $\Theta(n^2 2^n)$.
$(\log n)^2 2^n = o(n^2 2^n)$; there is no logarithm anywhere in the sum $\sum k$.
$4^n = 2^n \cdot 2^n$ grows much faster than $n^2 2^n$ since $2^n \gg n^2$.

cse-2025-1-cs-10.shortcut: Unroll: $T(n) = 2^n T(0) + \sum_{k=1}^{n} 2^{n-k} \cdot k2^k = 2^n\left(1 + \sum_{k=1}^n k\right)$ — every level contributes $k \cdot 2^n$.
pitfalls: Applying the master theorem: it does not apply to subtract-and-conquer recurrences like $T(n-1)$.
Stopping at $\Theta(n2^n)$ by looking only at the non-recursive term.
cse-2025-1-cs-10.verification: $T(1) = 2 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 2 = 4$ and the formula gives $2(1 + 1) = 4$; $T(2) = 2 \cdot 4 + 2 \cdot 4 = 16$ and the formula gives $4(1 + 3) = 16$.

cse-2025-1-cs-11.approach: Simulate the insertion: find the leaf for 23, see it is already full, split it and push a separator into the root, which is also full and splits too. Count nodes and levels before and after.

steps.title: Find the leaf for 23
steps.body: At the root, $23 \ge 19$, so follow the rightmost pointer to leaf $[20, 21, 22]$. It already has 3 keys (the maximum), so inserting 23 overflows it.

steps.title: Split the leaf, copy 22 up
steps.body: Split $[20, 21, 22, 23]$ into $[20, 21]$ and $[22, 23]$ and copy the first key of the new right leaf, 22, into the parent. The root becomes $[6, 12, 19, 22]$ — 4 keys, so the **root overflows** too.

scene.caption: Root now has 4 keys and 5 children

steps.title: Split the root, new root 19
steps.body: Split the internal node $[6, 12, 19, 22]$: left $[6, 12]$ (3 children), right $[22]$ (2 children), and the middle key 19 **moves up** into a brand-new root $[19]$. (Pushing 12 up instead, with $[6]$ and $[19, 22]$, gives the same counts.)

steps.title: Count the effects
steps.body:
- Splits happened (leaf and root) → (A) false, (B) true.
- Nodes: $5 \to 5 + 1 \text{ (leaf split)} + 1 \text{ (root split)} + 1 \text{ (new root)} = 8$ → (C) false.
- Levels: $2 \to 3$ because the root split created a new root → (D) true.

answer.value: **(B) and (D)**: nodes split, and the height grows from 2 to 3

optionAnalysis.reason: False: the target leaf $[20, 21, 22]$ is full, so it must split (and then the full root splits).
True: the leaf splits into $[20, 21]$ / $[22, 23]$ and the root splits into two internal nodes.
False: the node count rises from 5 to 8.
True: a split of the root always adds a new root, so the height increases by one (2 → 3).

cse-2025-1-cs-11.shortcut: Every node on the root-to-leaf path for 23 is full ($[6,12,19]$ and $[20,21,22]$), so the split propagates all the way up and the height must increase.
pitfalls: Assuming 23 can be redistributed to a sibling leaf: every leaf is full, and standard B+ tree insertion splits.
Being distracted by the unsorted first leaf (printed as 1, 4, 3): it is not on the insertion path and does not affect the result.
cse-2025-1-cs-11.verification: Whatever split convention is used (2–2 or 3–1 for the leaf; push 12 or 19 for the root), the path is entirely full, so both levels split and a new root appears: B and D hold, A and C fail.

cse-2025-1-cs-12.approach: Write down the three segments of the handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. Then read the SYN and ACK flags of each and test every option.

steps.title: P1: client sends SYN
steps.body: The client opens the connection with a segment carrying its initial sequence number: **SYN = 1**, ACK = 0 (nothing to acknowledge yet). So (D) "P1: SYN = 1" is true.

steps.title: P2: server replies SYN + ACK
steps.body: The server sends its own initial sequence number and acknowledges the client's SYN in the same segment: **SYN = 1, ACK = 1**. So (B) is true and (C) (SYN = 0) is false.

steps.title: P3: client sends ACK
steps.body: The client acknowledges the server's SYN: **SYN = 0, ACK = 1**. SYN is set only in the first segment from each side, so (A) "P3: SYN = 1, ACK = 1" is false.

optionAnalysis.reason: False: P3 is the final pure ACK; it has SYN = 0.
True: P2 is the SYN-ACK segment.
False: P2 must carry SYN = 1 to send the server's initial sequence number.
True: P1 is the SYN segment.

pitfalls: Thinking SYN stays set after the connection request: each side sets SYN exactly once (P1 for the client, P2 for the server).
cse-2025-1-cs-12.verification: The SYN flag consumes one sequence number per side: client SYN in P1, server SYN in P2 — exactly two SYN-flagged segments, both checked.

cse-2025-1-cs-13.approach: The coefficient determinant $1 - k^2$ is nonzero for all $k \ne \pm 1$ (unique solution). Check the two singular values $k = 1$ and $k = -1$ separately for inconsistency vs. dependence.

steps.title: Determinant of the coefficient matrix
steps.body:
$$\det\begin{pmatrix} 1 & k \\ k & 1 \end{pmatrix} = 1 \cdot 1 - k \cdot k = 1 - k^2.$$
For every $k \ne \pm 1$ it is nonzero, so the system has **exactly one solution** — for infinitely many $k$.

steps.title: k = 1: no solution
steps.body: The equations become $x + y = 1$ and $x + y = -1$: the same left side equals two different numbers, a contradiction. **No solution.**

steps.title: k = −1: infinitely many solutions
steps.body: The equations become $x - y = 1$ and $-x + y = -1$. The second is $(-1) \times$ the first, so only one independent equation remains: $y = x - 1$ — **infinitely many solutions**.

steps.title: Score the options
steps.body:
- No solution only for $k = 1$: exactly one value → (A) true, (B) false.
- Unique solution for all $k \ne \pm 1$: infinitely many values → (C) false.
- Infinitely many solutions only for $k = -1$ → (D) true.

optionAnalysis.reason: True: only $k = 1$ gives an inconsistent system.
False: inconsistency needs $1 - k^2 = 0$, which has just two roots, and only $k = 1$ is inconsistent.
False: every $k \ne \pm 1$ gives a unique solution — infinitely many such $k$, not exactly one.
True: only $k = -1$ makes the two equations multiples of each other.

cse-2025-1-cs-13.shortcut: Ratio test: $\frac{1}{k} = \frac{k}{1}$ gives $k = \pm 1$. For $k = 1$ the left sides coincide but the constants are $1$ and $-1$ (parallel lines, no solution); for $k = -1$ the second equation is $-1$ times the first (same line, infinitely many).
pitfalls: Declaring both $k = \pm 1$ as "no solution" without checking the constants — $k = -1$ gives coincident lines.
cse-2025-1-cs-13.verification: At $k = -1$, $(x, y) = (1, 0)$ and $(2, 1)$ both satisfy $x - y = 1$ and $-x + y = -1$; at $k = 1$, adding $x+y=1$ and $-(x+y)=1$ gives $0 = 2$.

cse-2025-1-cs-14.approach: $X$ is the 3-input majority function. Use its key property $X(p, p, q) = p$ (two equal inputs decide), split into cases $a = b$ / $a \ne b$ (or $a = c$ / $a \ne c$) to prove identities, and give one assignment to refute the false ones.
cse-2025-1-cs-14.given: $X(p, q, r) = pq + qr + pr$ (output 1 iff at least two inputs are 1). Key facts: $X(p, p, q) = p$ and $X$ is symmetric in its inputs.

steps.title: Option (B) is true: case on a, b
steps.body:
- If $a = b$: LHS $= X(a, a, \cdot) = a$ and RHS $= X(a, a, c) = a$. Equal.
- If $a \ne b$: one of $a, b$ is 1 and the other 0, so $X(a, b, z) = z$ for any $z$. LHS $= X(a, b, c)$ = RHS.

So $X(a, b, X(a, b, c)) = X(a, b, c)$ always.

steps.title: Option (C) is false: a counterexample
steps.body:
$X(a, b, a) = a$ and $X(c, d, c) = c$, so RHS $= a \text{ AND } c$.
Take $a = b = 1$, $c = d = 0$: LHS $= X(1, 1, X(1,0,0)) = X(1,1,0) = 1$, RHS $= 1 \text{ AND } 0 = 0$. Not equal.

steps.title: Option (D) is true: case on a, c
steps.body:
$X(a, c, c) = c$, so RHS $= X(a, X(a, b, c), c)$.
- If $a = c$: $X(a, b, c) = X(a, b, a) = a$, and RHS $= X(a, a, a) = a$ = LHS.
- If $a \ne c$: $X(a, b, c) = b$ (the tie-breaker), and RHS $= X(a, b, c)$ = LHS.

So (D) is an identity.

optionAnalysis.reason: False: majority is not associative in this sense; $a = b = 1$, $c = d = e = 0$ gives LHS 1, RHS 0.
True: if $a = b$ both sides equal $a$; if $a \ne b$, $X(a, b, z) = z$, so both sides equal $X(a, b, c)$.
False: RHS reduces to $a \cdot c$, but with $a = b = 1$, $c = d = 0$ LHS is 1 and RHS is 0.
True: $X(a, c, c) = c$; then the cases $a = c$ and $a \ne c$ both give $X(a, b, c)$.

cse-2025-1-cs-14.shortcut: Remember: with two inputs equal, majority returns that value; with two inputs different, it returns the third. Every identity here collapses in one line with this rule.
pitfalls: Treating majority like AND/OR and assuming associativity (option A).
Forgetting $X(p, p, q) = p$, which makes (C)'s right side just $a \cdot c$.
cse-2025-1-cs-14.verification: Exhaustive check over all 8 assignments of $(a, b, c)$ for (B) and (D) (with $d$ irrelevant): both sides agree in every row, matching the case proofs.

cse-2025-1-cs-15.approach: Widening a 2's complement number is **sign extension**: copy the sign bit into every new high-order bit. $-6 = 1010$ has sign bit 1, so pad with 1s.

steps.title: Why padding with a single 1 then 0s is wrong
steps.body: (A) $1000\,1010 = 138 - 256 = -118$. (C) $1000\,0000\,0000\,1010 = 32778 - 65536 = -32758$. Putting 0s in the new positions is sign–magnitude thinking, not 2's complement.

optionAnalysis.reason: Pads with 0s after the leading 1: value $-128 + 10 = -118$, not $-6$.
Correct sign extension: $-256 + 250 = -6$.
Same mistake in 16 bits: $-32768 + 10 = -32758$.
Correct sign extension: $-65536 + 65530 = -6$.

cse-2025-1-cs-15.shortcut: $-6$ in any width is "all 1s except the low bits of $+5$ inverted": $+6 = \ldots 0110$, invert $\ldots 1001$, add 1 $\to \ldots 1010$ with 1s above. Any option with 0s above bit 3 is wrong.
pitfalls: Moving only the sign bit to the new MSB and filling with 0s (that is sign–magnitude extension).

cse-2025-1-cs-16.approach: Test each statement against the BST definition and the two extreme shapes: the skewed chain (worst case) and a node with a left child (heap order fails).

steps.title: (A) Longest root-to-node path is n − 1
steps.body: A path from the root visits distinct nodes, so it has at most $n$ nodes, i.e. at most $n - 1$ edges. Inserting $1, 2, 3, 4$ in order gives a chain where the path to the deepest node has exactly $n - 1 = 3$ edges. So the maximum length is $n - 1$: **true**.

steps.title: (B) Inorder traversal is sorted
steps.body: Inorder visits left subtree, root, right subtree. By the BST property every key on the left is smaller and every key on the right is larger, so by induction the output is in increasing order: **true**.

steps.title: (C) Search is O(log n) in the worst case?
steps.body: In the skewed chain, searching for 4 compares with $1, 2, 3, 4$: $n$ comparisons, so the worst case is $\Theta(n)$, not $O(\log_2 n)$. $O(\log n)$ holds only for balanced BSTs (AVL, red-black): **false**.

steps.title: (D) Every BST is a min-heap?
steps.body: A min-heap needs every parent $\le$ its children. In the BST with root 2 and left child 1, the parent 2 is larger than its child 1 — heap order fails (and a BST need not be a complete tree either): **false**.
